label: Person
name: Giuseppe Garibaldi
summary:
Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807–1882) was an Italian general, patriot, and republican who played a central role in the unification of Italy. Known as the 'Hero of Two Worlds,' he fought for liberation movements in South America before leading the legendary Expedition of the Thousand that conquered the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1860.

Born in Nice (then part of the Kingdom of Sardinia), Garibaldi joined Giuseppe Mazzini's Young Italy movement and was sentenced to death in absentia in 1834. He fled to South America, where he fought for the Riograndense Republic in Brazil and defended Montevideo against Argentine forces, earning international fame as a guerrilla commander.

Returning to Italy in 1848, Garibaldi fought in the First Italian War of Independence and briefly led the Roman Republic's defense against French forces. His greatest triumph came in 1860 when his volunteer force of roughly 1,000 Redshirts sailed from Genoa, conquered Sicily and Naples, and handed the entire southern half of Italy to King Victor Emmanuel II.

Garibaldi's selfless surrender of conquered territory to the Sardinian monarchy—rather than claiming power for himself—made him an icon of republican virtue. Abraham Lincoln offered him a Union command in the American Civil War, and he remains Italy's most beloved national hero.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand led to the unification of Italy in 1860, uniting a fragmented peninsula under one government for the first time since the fall of the Roman Empire. This event had significant regional and continental implications, contributing to the redrawing of European borders.
